newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Popular support for Zaire rebels said growing.
newsitem.headline: Popular support for Zaire rebels said growing.

text.p: Popular support for rebels battling the Zaire government is growing, notably in areas looted by retreating Zairean soldiers, local residents say.
In Kindu, the latest major town seized by rebels in eastern Zaire, youths jammed guerrilla centres on Thursday to enlist in the force that has put the Zaire army to flight.
Overwhelmed rebel leaders turned away youths.
Reports from the southern mining province of Shaba pointed on Thursday for the first time to a groundswell of support for the guerrillas in at least parts of the separatist region.

Local Zaireans in the town of Manono deep in the copper-rich province declared it "rebel-held territory" during a rally on Monday after a scuffle with local gendarmes, three different sources in the region told Reuters.
The defence ministry and state radio denied the town had been taken by rebels.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his forces took Manono on Monday but it was not clear whether his guerrillas had actually arrived there.

"The local population rose up and forced 11 gendarmes stationed there to leave, and then declared the town to be rebel-held territory," one resident of the provincial capital, Lubumbashi, in radio contact with Manono told Reuters.
Two other sources in contact with the region corroborated the account.

The defence ministry in Kinshasa confirmed that young members of the UFERI party, a federalist group with strong backing in Shaba, had declared their intention to welcome the rebels at Manono during a rally on Monday.
But it denied that gendarmes had left the town. State radio broadcast government denials on Thursday night saying the town had never fallen to rebels.

"This news is alarmist. What happened was there was a scuffle between the UFERI youth and the gendarmes. The UFERI youth said during a rally they were preparing for Kabila to come. But the gendarmes are still there and there is no sign of the rebels," a defence ministry spokesman told Reuters.
Kindu, on the western bank of the Zaire river, is the westernmost town seized by the rebels who have captured a stretch of the east 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October.
Efforts by foreign mercenaries to bolster the ramshackle army of President Mobutu Sese Seko have failed because of poor logistics, training and low morale among troops.
In contrast, rebel ranks have been swollen by thousands of youths from captured areas who scent victory and opportunity with the northwest capital of Kisangani in the rebel sights.
Both the government and the rebels drifted further apart on Thursday on the question of a ceasefire.

The rebels thrusting deeper in eastern Zaire rejected the government's call for international monitors to help implement a U.N. truce plan. The government in turn again ruled out negotiations between the ailing Mobutu and Kabila.

The rebel leader links a truce to such talks, which he says should centre only on negotiating an end to Mobutu's 31-year rule in the Central African nation. Mobutu has been in Europe for cancer treatment for most of the time since last August.

"Kabila is a mere puppet. How can President Mobutu negotiate with him while it's known that he is only a front man for the aggressors," Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka told reporters in the capital Kinshasa.
Zaire accuses Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of fomenting the conflict and of sending their regular troops to help the rebels. All three neighbours deny involvement.
